orig_9709_m1_mom_signed.description: Use one positive direction, calculate the momentum of each particle and combine signed contributions on a straight line.

sections.title: How does momentum depend on mass and velocity?
sections.label: Use mass times velocity
sections.intro: Momentum is a vector. Along one line, a sign can record its direction once an axis has been chosen.

blocks.html: \(p=mv\). A positive mass never changes the sign: the momentum points in the same physical direction as the velocity.

figure.alt: A positive axis points right. One trolley moves left and has a negative contribution. A second moves right and has a positive contribution.
figure.caption: Pick a positive arrow first. Each momentum then has the sign of its velocity.

blocks.html: The speed may be positive even when the signed momentum is negative.

blocks.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle
blocks.prompt:
A particle has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) and moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give its signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Rightward is positive. The signed momentum has the same sign as the velocity.

blocks.hint: Use velocity including the sign, and convert the mass to kilograms.
blocks.solution:
The mass is already in kilograms and the signed velocity is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Apply \(p=mv\). The result is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Use masses in \(\mathrm{kg}\), signed velocities in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Which units must I use before multiplying?
sections.label: Convert the mass first
sections.intro: Convert grams to kilograms before using an SI velocity. Show the conversion next to the value.

blocks.html: \(1000\,\mathrm g=1\,\mathrm{kg}\). The usual momentum unit is \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
Using a number in grams in the kilogram calculation makes the momentum a thousand times too large.

blocks.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle
blocks.prompt:
A particle has mass \(320\,\mathrm g\) and moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give its signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Rightward is positive. The signed momentum has the same sign as the velocity.

blocks.hint: Use velocity including the sign, and convert the mass to kilograms.
blocks.solution:
Convert \(320\,\mathrm g\) to \(\frac{8}{25}\,\mathrm{kg}\) before multiplying.

Apply \(p=mv\). The result is \(\frac{8}{5}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: What if the velocity or mass is missing?
sections.label: Rearrange the definition
sections.intro: Use the known signed momentum with the appropriate rearrangement. If the particle is moving, a mass found from signed quantities must be positive.

blocks.html: \(v=\frac{p}{m}\). If \(v\ne0\), \(m=\frac{p}{v}\). A stationary particle has zero momentum for every positive mass.
For a left-moving particle both its signed velocity and signed momentum are negative. Their quotient is positive.

blocks.title: Recover velocity from momentum
blocks.prompt:
Take rightward as positive.

A particle has mass \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{kg}\) and signed momentum \(-9\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). Give its signed velocity in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Rearrange the definition p equals mass times signed velocity.
blocks.solution:
Divide momentum by mass: \(v=\frac{-9}{\frac{3}{2}}=-6\).

The negative sign indicates leftward motion.

sections.title: When do the two contributions cancel?
sections.label: Add signed components
sections.intro: Find the momentum of each particle independently. Then add the two signed values.

blocks.html: For two particles on one line, \(P=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B\). Use one positive direction for both.

QuantitySigned interpretation
PositiveAlong the positive axis.
ZeroNo total along the axis.
NegativeOpposite to the positive axis.
Add signed components rather than speeds or momentum magnitudes.

blocks.title: Add momenta using one positive direction
blocks.prompt:
Particles A and B have masses \(\frac{4}{5}\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Use rightward as positive. Give the total signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Adding the magnitudes loses the direction. Add the signed components.

blocks.hint: Decide the sign of each velocity before multiplying by its mass.
blocks.solution:
With rightward positive, the two momentum components are \(4\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(-6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

Add the signed values to get \(-2\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Can moving particles have zero total momentum?
sections.label: Balance signed contributions
sections.intro: Two signed contributions can cancel, even while both particles are moving. An individual momentum need not be zero.

blocks.html: Zero total means \(m_Av_A=-m_Bv_B\). With nonzero values, the directions are opposite and the magnitudes agree.
Equal and opposite momenta can belong to particles with different speeds if their masses differ.

blocks.title: Find the velocity that balances total momentum
blocks.prompt:
Particles A and B have masses \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the left at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The two particles have zero total momentum.

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Zero total momentum means the two signed momenta add to zero.
blocks.solution:
A contributes \(-24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). B must contribute the opposite component.

\[(4)(-6)+(3)v_B=0\]

\(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: What changes if I choose the opposite direction?
sections.label: Reverse the sign convention
sections.intro: The physical direction stays fixed. Reversing the positive axis changes the sign of every component at the same time.

blocks.html: A sign reversal changes the description rather than the motion. State the convention so the result can be interpreted.
Do not reverse the sign of only one term if changing the axis for the whole system.

blocks.title: Add momenta using one positive direction
blocks.prompt:
Particles A and B have masses \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Use leftward as positive. Give the total signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Adding the magnitudes loses the direction. Add the signed components.

blocks.hint: Decide the sign of each velocity before multiplying by its mass.
blocks.solution:
With leftward positive, the two momentum components are \(-24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(15\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

Add the signed values to get \(-9\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle

examples.title: Recover positive mass from signed data
examples.question:
Take rightward as positive.

A particle moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and its signed momentum is \(-12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its mass in kilograms.
solution: Use the signed velocity \(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its sign is the same as the given momentum.
\(m=\frac{-12}{-3}=4\), which is positive.

examples.title: Add momenta using one positive direction
examples.question:

Add the signed values to get \(2\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.question:

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
solution: A contributes \(30\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). B must contribute the opposite component.
\(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Add momenta using one positive direction
examples.question:
Particles A and B have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

solution: With leftward positive, the two momentum components are \(6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(-10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
Add the signed values to get \(-4\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

glossary.definition: One-dimensional velocity measured using a chosen positive direction.
The sum of the signed momenta of the particles in the system.

orig_9709_m1_mom_direct.description: Set up a signed momentum equation before and after direct impact, then recover missing velocities or a mass from the stated data.

sections.title: When can I conserve total momentum?
sections.label: Choose a system and axis
sections.intro: Choose both colliding bodies. Their mutual forces transfer momentum within the pair. On a smooth horizontal line there is no external horizontal force in the model.

blocks.html: \(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B\), with \(u\) just before, \(v\) just after.

figure.alt: Two rows show a left particle approaching a stationary right particle, followed by both particles moving right with the right particle moving faster.
figure.caption: The positive direction stays the same before and after the impact.

blocks.html:
StageAB
Before\(m_Au_A\)\(m_Bu_B\)
After\(m_Av_A\)\(m_Bv_B\)
Individual momenta usually change. Conservation applies to the sum for the selected pair.

blocks.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{9}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Keep the signed result. A negative velocity means motion to the left.

blocks.hint: Multiply each signed velocity by its own mass before adding.
blocks.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(21\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(7)+(4)(0)=(4)v+(3)(\frac{9}{7})\]

Hence \(v=\frac{30}{7}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{30}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: How do I use a particle that starts at rest?
sections.label: Find a missing final velocity
sections.intro: A stationary particle contributes zero initially. It can still contribute a final momentum after impact.

blocks.html: Substitute the known final contribution, then subtract it from the previously calculated total.
A zero initial velocity does not remove that mass from the final equation.

blocks.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, B moves to the right at \(\frac{56}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Keep the signed result. A negative velocity means motion to the left.

blocks.hint: Multiply each signed velocity by its own mass before adding.
blocks.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(36\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(4)(9)+(5)(0)=(4)v+(5)(\frac{56}{9})\]

Hence \(v=\frac{11}{9}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{11}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Where must I show the change of direction?
sections.label: Handle opposite motion and rebound
sections.intro: A speed and a direction together determine a signed velocity. Put in the sign before writing the momentum equation.

blocks.html: After finding a negative signed velocity, state the non-negative speed with the direction if the question requests both.
A particle can change direction during the collision. Re-use the fixed axis instead of re-using the old sign.

blocks.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after impact, B moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the speed of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and select its direction.
blocks.hint: Multiply each signed velocity by its own mass before adding.
blocks.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(7\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(4)+(5)(-1)=(3)v+(5)(2)\]

Hence \(v=-1\). The particle moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Can I find an initial velocity from the final state?
sections.label: Work backwards
sections.intro: Either total can be calculated first. Start from the side with no missing contributions.

blocks.html: Equate the known total to the side which has the unknown initial velocity.
The sign of an initial velocity need not match the sign after impact.

blocks.title: Work backwards from final motion
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The masses of A and B are \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{23}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(\frac{51}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use the velocity before impact.
blocks.hint: Calculate the known final total before solving for the initial velocity.
blocks.solution:
After impact the total momentum is \(31\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[5u+(2)(-2)=31\]

Solving gives \(u=7\). The resulting initial velocities show A approaching B.

sections.title: Where does an unknown mass occur?
sections.label: Collect the mass terms
sections.intro: If the mass remains constant, the same unknown participates before and after. Factor it out after moving those terms together.

blocks.html: \(m_A(u_A-v_A)=m_B(v_B-u_B)\). Check that the calculated mass is positive.
Use changes in signed velocity rather than differences of speeds.

blocks.title: Recover a mass from collision data
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The mass of B is \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the right at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) before impact. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{37}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(\frac{51}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the mass of A in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Collect together the terms involving the unknown mass before dividing.
blocks.solution:
Set the total momentum before equal to the total afterwards.

\[(3)(\frac{44}{7})=m(\frac{33}{7})\]

Solving gives the positive mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\).

sections.title: What if both final velocities are unknown?
sections.label: Use the second piece of data
sections.intro: A known difference or a stated ratio between final velocities supplies a second equation. The ordering helps interpret the signs.

blocks.html: Write the relation using signed velocities. If the condition is a ratio of speeds, use the stated directions to remove the absolute values.
The momentum equation alone permits more than one pair of final velocities.

blocks.title: Use a second condition for two velocities
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact B moves at a signed velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) greater than A's signed velocity.

Give both signed velocities immediately after impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the relation between the two velocities alongside momentum conservation.
blocks.solution:
Momentum alone gives \(3v_A+4v_B=0\).

Write \(v_B=v_A+2\) and substitute it in the momentum equation.

Solving the two conditions gives \(v_A=- \frac{8}{7}\) and \(v_B=\frac{6}{7}\), in metres per second.

The right-hand particle has the greater signed final velocity. The gap opens.

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
solution: Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

solution: Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.question:

Give the speed of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and select its direction.
solution: Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
Hence \(v=- \frac{5}{7}\). The particle moves to the left at \(\frac{5}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after impact, A is at rest.

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
solution: Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
Hence \(v=3\). The particle moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Work backwards from final motion
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The masses of A and B are \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use the velocity before impact.
solution: After impact the total momentum is \(18\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
Solving gives \(u=2\). The resulting initial velocities show A approaching B.

examples.title: Recover a mass from collision data
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The mass of A is \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) before impact. Immediately after impact, A moves to the left at \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the mass of B in kilograms.
solution: Set the total momentum before equal to the total afterwards.
Solving gives the positive mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

examples.title: Use a second condition for two velocities
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact B moves at a signed velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) greater than A's signed velocity.

Give both signed velocities immediately after impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
solution: Momentum alone gives \(4v_A+6v_B=8\).
Write \(v_B=v_A+3\) and substitute it in the momentum equation.
Solving the two conditions gives \(v_A=-1\) and \(v_B=2\), in metres per second.
The right-hand particle has the greater signed final velocity. The gap opens.

extraPractice.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
extraPractice.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{9}{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

retry.feedback: Keep the signed result. A negative velocity means motion to the left.

extraPractice.hint: Multiply each signed velocity by its own mass before adding.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(8)+(5)(0)=(5)v+(3)(\frac{9}{8})\]

Hence \(v=\frac{33}{8}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{33}{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

extraPractice.hint: Multiply each signed velocity by its own mass before adding.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(-25\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(4)(-1)+(3)(-7)=(4)v+(3)(- \frac{17}{7})\]

extraPractice.title: Work backwards from final motion
extraPractice.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The masses of A and B are \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, B moves to the left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact, A moves to the left at \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

extraPractice.hint: Calculate the known final total before solving for the initial velocity.
extraPractice.solution:
After impact the total momentum is \(-5\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[3u+(5)(-4)=-5\]

Solving gives \(u=5\). The resulting initial velocities show A approaching B.

extraPractice.title: Recover a mass from collision data
extraPractice.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

The mass of A is \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) before impact. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(\frac{13}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the mass of B in kilograms.
extraPractice.hint: Collect together the terms involving the unknown mass before dividing.
extraPractice.solution:
Set the total momentum before equal to the total afterwards.

\[(4)(\frac{11}{3})=m(\frac{22}{3})\]

Solving gives the positive mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\).

extraPractice.title: Use a second condition for two velocities
extraPractice.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. After impact A moves left and B moves right. B's speed is \(\frac{16}{5}\) times A's speed.

orig_9709_m1_mom_coalescence.description: Combine the masses when two particles stick, calculate their shared velocity and work backwards from a stated common motion.

sections.title: What changes when the two particles stick?
sections.label: One shared final velocity
sections.intro: Before impact two velocities can differ. If the particles stick, they have one common velocity immediately afterwards.

blocks.html: \(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=(m_A+m_B)v\). The common velocity carries a sign.

figure.alt: Cart A moves towards stationary cart B. After contact they share a single box and one velocity arrow.
figure.caption: Keep separate before terms. Combine the masses after they join.

blocks.html: Do not divide by only one mass. Both move with the final velocity.

blocks.title: Find a shared final velocity
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest.

Give the signed velocity of the joined pair in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Signed velocity of the joined pair

blocks.hint: Use a single final velocity for the combined mass.
blocks.solution:
Since the particles stick, their common velocity \(v\) is multiplied by the combined mass \(9\,\mathrm{kg}\).

\[(4)(7)+(5)(0)=28=9v\]

\(\frac{28}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{28}{9}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Which way does the joined pair move?
sections.label: Opposing contributions
sections.intro: When the initial velocities point in opposite directions, one signed momentum contribution is negative.

blocks.html: The direction of common motion follows the sign of the total initial momentum under the chosen convention.
The heavier particle need not determine the direction on its own. The product of mass and velocity determines each contribution.

blocks.title: Find a shared final velocity
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

Give the signed velocity of the joined pair in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Signed velocity of the joined pair

blocks.hint: Use a single final velocity for the combined mass.
blocks.solution:
Since the particles stick, their common velocity \(v\) is multiplied by the combined mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\).

\[(2)(5)+(6)(-4)=-14=8v\]

\(- \frac{7}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the left at \(\frac{7}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: When can both particles end up at rest?
sections.label: Cancel the two momenta
sections.intro: A stationary joined body has zero final momentum. The individual velocities before impact need not be zero.

blocks.html: Set \(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=0\) if the particles coalesce and stop.
A zero total before a non-coalescing impact would not be enough to conclude that both particles come to rest.

blocks.title: Determine the mass needed to stop
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Afterwards the joined pair is at rest.

Find the mass of B in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Keep the unknown mass in both the before and after expressions.
blocks.solution:
Write the final momentum as \((3+m)(0)\).

\[(3)(8)+m(-3)=(3+m)(0)\]

Collecting gives \(m(3)=24\). Therefore \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\).

sections.title: How can the common velocity reveal missing data?
sections.label: Recover an initial velocity
sections.intro: Calculate the two-mass total after impact first. Use it as the known total when constructing the equation before impact.

blocks.html: For an unknown initial velocity, subtract the other contribution and divide by the mass of the corresponding particle.
Use the combined mass only for the final total. Divide by the mass of the particle whose initial velocity is missing.

blocks.title: Find an initial velocity from coalescence
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A and B have masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, B moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Afterwards the joined pair moves to the right at \(\frac{11}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Find the signed initial velocity of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Work back from the known common velocity.
blocks.solution:
The total after impact is \(22\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[3u+(5)(-1)=22\]

Solving gives \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Does an unknown mass occur on both sides?
sections.label: Collect mass terms
sections.intro: An unknown mass is present before impact and in the total mass afterwards. Expand only enough to collect the terms involving it.

blocks.html: \(m_B(v-u_B)=m_A(u_A-v)\). Check positivity after solving.
Subtract the original signed velocity of B before dividing. A negative initial velocity contributes a plus when subtracted.

blocks.title: Find an unknown mass after coalescence
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Afterwards the joined pair moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Find the mass of B in kilograms.
blocks.hint: Keep the unknown mass in both the before and after expressions.
blocks.solution:
Write the final momentum as \((2+m)(-1)\).

\[(2)(6)+m(-3)=(2+m)(-1)\]

Collecting gives \(m(2)=14\). Therefore \(7\,\mathrm{kg}\).

sections.title: What can I check before trusting the result?
sections.label: Use the weighted mean
sections.intro: The common velocity is a weighted mean of the two initial velocities. Both masses are positive.

blocks.html: When the initial velocities differ, the common velocity is strictly between them. Momentum conservation determines exactly where it lies.

ObservationCheck
Equal weightsOrdinary mean of the two initial velocities.
Opposite totalCommon direction follows the signed sum.
Outlying final valueIncompatible with positive masses.
A value between the initial velocities can still be wrong. Check the exact totals.

blocks.title: Test a report about the joined pair

blocks.hint: Being between the initial velocities is a quick check. The exact momentum test gives the final answer.
blocks.solution:
The total initially is \(20\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). The total for the reported state would be \(20\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

It gives the same total momentum as the initial motion.

Using the combined mass gives \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: How do I know which particles can meet?
sections.label: Compare the signed velocities
sections.intro: With A to the left of B, the rate at which the positive gap closes is the velocity of A minus that of B.

blocks.html: If \(v_A>v_B\), the gap closes. This rule also works if both are moving left.

figure.alt: The first row shows a left and right particle with the left signed velocity greater. The second row shows the order after impact with the right signed velocity greater.
figure.caption: Compare signed velocities in position order. The left particle need not be moving right.

blocks.html: The two particles may be travelling in the same direction and still approach one another.

blocks.title: Calculate the rate at which the gap closes
blocks.prompt:
At one instant A is \(5\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed closing rate, defined as \(v_A-v_B\), in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Decide what the gap then does if velocities are constant.
blocks.hint: Use left velocity minus right velocity regardless of the directions of travel.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the right-hand velocity from the left-hand velocity: \((-4)-(-7)=3\).

The two particles approach.

sections.title: Can I turn the closing rate into a contact time?
sections.label: Calculate a positive time
sections.intro: At constant velocities, each second closes the same amount of gap. If the gap starts positive, a later contact needs a positive closing rate.

blocks.html: For initial gap \(d>0\) and \(v_A>v_B\), time to contact is \(\frac{d}{v_A-v_B}\).
Zero or negative closing rate means there is no later contact while the velocities stay fixed.

blocks.title: Test whether the gap closes
blocks.prompt:
A is \(8\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the right at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at constant velocities.

Take rightward as positive.

Decide whether they meet. If they meet, give the time to contact in seconds.
blocks.hint: Subtract the signed right-particle velocity from the signed left-particle velocity.
blocks.solution:
The signed rate at which the gap closes is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The left particle must have a greater signed velocity to make contact.

Divide the starting gap \(8\,\mathrm m\) by the positive closing rate to obtain \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm s\).

sections.title: What changes after a separating collision?
sections.label: Check the gap opens
sections.intro: Immediately after a separating direct collision, the right particle moves away faster along the signed axis than the left particle.

blocks.html: Check \(v_B-v_A>0\). A zero gap-opening rate alone does not prove that the bodies joined.

StageTest for A left of B
Approach\(u_A>u_B\)
Separation\(v_A<v_B\)
Common speed\(v_A=v_B\)
Calculating a positive gap-opening rate does not replace the momentum check.

blocks.title: Compare a collision report with two requirements
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A and B have masses \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

A report describes the immediate state afterwards as follows. A moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Which tests pass: matching total momentum, and an immediate opening of the gap?
blocks.hint: Test conserved momentum and the ordering of final velocities separately.
blocks.solution:
Before and proposed after totals are \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). They match.

The proposed gap-opening rate is \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is positive.

Both tests pass.

sections.title: What can be wrong with recorded data?
sections.label: Check two requirements independently
sections.intro: A pair of proposed velocities can pass one check and fail the other. Compute the momentum totals and the signed gap-opening rate separately.

blocks.html: Require both an equal total and a positive gap-opening rate if the stated outcome is a separating collision.
Do not reject an otherwise possible result simply because one velocity is negative.

blocks.title: Compare a collision report with two requirements
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A and B have masses \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

A report describes the immediate state afterwards as follows. A is at rest. B moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Which tests pass: matching total momentum, and an immediate opening of the gap?
blocks.hint: Test conserved momentum and the ordering of final velocities separately.
blocks.solution:
Before and proposed after totals are \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). They match.

The proposed gap-opening rate is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is positive.

Both tests pass.

sections.title: How do I use a direction-dependent speed condition?
sections.label: Turn a ratio into a signed equation
sections.intro: Use the stated directions first. A negative signed velocity represents a positive speed equal to its magnitude.

blocks.html: When A moves left and B moves right, a positive speed ratio \(k\) gives \(v_B=-kv_A\). Use the momentum equation with this relation.
Writing a positive multiplier between velocities would predict the same direction.

blocks.title: Use a second condition for two velocities
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact A moves left and B moves right. B's speed is \(\frac{8}{7}\) times A's speed.

Give both signed velocities immediately after impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the relation between the two velocities alongside momentum conservation.
blocks.solution:
Momentum alone gives \(2v_A+3v_B=2\).

For \(v_A<0<v_B\), their ratio of non-negative speeds gives \(v_B=-\frac{8}{7}v_A\).

Solving the two conditions gives \(v_A=- \frac{7}{5}\) and \(v_B=\frac{8}{5}\), in metres per second.

The right-hand particle has the greater signed final velocity. The gap opens.

sections.title: What can I deduce with only a separation condition?
sections.label: Find the strict interval
sections.intro: With one momentum equation and an ordering inequality, the exact values may still be unknown. State what the two conditions imply.

blocks.html: For known total \(P\), the sign condition for separation forces \(v_A<\frac P{m_A+m_B}\) after substituting the momentum equation.
With equality the gap stops opening. Include the boundary only if the question explicitly allows it.

blocks.title: Find the interval allowed by separation
blocks.prompt:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The post-collision signed velocity of A is \(v\). Use only momentum conservation and the fact that the gap opens immediately. Give the resulting inequality in \(v\).

retry.feedback: Equality gives the same final velocity. The question requires an opening gap.

blocks.hint: The right particle must have the larger signed final velocity.
blocks.solution:
Conservation gives \(v_B=\frac{16-(5)v}{3}\).

The gap opens when \(v_B>v\), so \(16-(5)v>3v\).

This gives \(v<2\). Equality would give no immediate gap increase.

examples.title: Calculate the rate at which the gap closes
examples.question:
At one instant A is \(3\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed closing rate, defined as \(v_A-v_B\), in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Decide what the gap then does if velocities are constant.
solution: Subtract the right-hand velocity from the left-hand velocity: \((2)-(1)=1\).
The two particles approach.

examples.title: Find the interval allowed by separation
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest.

The gap opens when \(v_B>v\), so \(12-(2)v>4v\).
This gives \(v<2\). Equality would give no immediate gap increase.

glossary.definition: \(v_A-v_B\) when A is left of B.
The right side's signed velocity exceeds the left side's: \(v_B>v_A\).
The position of the right particle minus that of the left particle.

revision.body:
Keep the particle order visible

Use one convention throughout. Let A be to the left of B.

StageCondition
Before contact\(u_A>u_B\) means the gap is closing.
Afterwards\(v_B>v_A\) means the gap is opening.
Given gap dTime \(\frac{d}{u_A-u_B}\) if the closing rate is positive.
Data checkCompare both signed momentum totals as well as the motion.
revision.checks:
• Check relative signed velocities rather than absolute speeds.
  • Equal signed velocities keep a gap constant.
  • A strict opening condition excludes equality.
revision.examTip: Write one sentence giving the reason for your conclusion about contact or separation.

orig_9709_m1_mom_successive.description: Track a changed velocity through two separate direct impacts, use each pair’s momentum and check a possible later contact.

sections.title: Which two particles belong in each equation?
sections.label: Separate the impacts
sections.intro: During an impact choose the pair actually in contact. Record another line of data for the next pair. The updated state in between matters.

blocks.html: For A–B use the two velocities just before and just after that impact. For B–C use the updated velocity of B and the still-current velocity of C.

figure.alt: The upper row shows the initial order A, B, C. The middle row shows the impact between A and B. The lower row shows the later impact between B and C.
figure.caption: Between impacts A keeps its updated velocity and B approaches C.

blocks.html:
EventOutgoing state to carry forward
A–B impactA and B now have updated velocities; C is unchanged.
B–C impactB and C update again; A keeps its earlier result.
Do not use the original velocity of B twice. Its momentum changes when A first hits it.

blocks.title: Carry the updated velocity to a second impact
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after the B–C impact, C moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B after each impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Signed velocity of B after A–B
Signed velocity of B after B–C

retry.feedback: That is the velocity after the first impact. Recalculate B with the data from the B–C impact.

blocks.hint: Use the final velocity of one stage as the initial velocity of the next.
blocks.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(20\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(3)+(2)u=20\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact the momentum of B and C just before contact is \(14\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)v+(2)(5)=14\]

B leaves this impact with signed velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The measured velocity of C was \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: How soon can the second impact occur?
sections.label: Time to the next contact
sections.intro: Use the current separation with the current velocity difference. Both come from the end of the first impact.

blocks.html: With B to the left of C and their velocities constant, a positive closing rate gives time \(\frac{\text{B--C gap}}{v_B-v_C}\).
A closing-rate calculation must use positions at the same moment and a consistent velocity sign.

blocks.title: Calculate the time between the two first impacts
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{11}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the first impact the gap between B and C is \(9\,\mathrm m\).

Give the time in seconds from the A–B impact to the B–C impact.
blocks.hint: First find B’s signed velocity at the end of the A–B impact, then calculate the B–C closing rate.
blocks.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(20\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(\frac{11}{5})+(3)u=20\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(\frac{26}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

The signed closing rate for B and C is \(\frac{26}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Dividing the gap by this rate gives \(\frac{45}{26}\,\mathrm s\).

sections.title: What changes if the second pair sticks?
sections.label: Allow for a joined body
sections.intro: If B and C coalesce, the after term uses their combined mass and one velocity. A stays separate until there is another contact.

blocks.html: The common final velocity becomes the velocity of the nearer joined body for any later contact test involving A.
Do not assign one shared velocity to all three particles. Only the bodies that stick share an after velocity.

blocks.title: Carry the updated velocity to a second impact
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B and C stick together at their impact.

Give the signed velocity of B after each impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Signed velocity of B after A–B
Signed velocity of B after B–C

retry.feedback: That is the velocity after the first impact. Recalculate B with the data from the B–C impact.

blocks.hint: Use the final velocity of one stage as the initial velocity of the next.
blocks.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(30\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(3)+(3)u=30\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact conserve momentum for B and C. The pair arrives with total \(27\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3+6)v=27\]

The joined B–C pair moves with signed velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Can A reach the particle in front again?
sections.label: Test the latest gap rate
sections.intro: A is still to the left at the second impact because A and B separated after their first impact. The question now is whether A can close that new gap.

blocks.html: Compare the unchanged velocity of A with B’s new velocity just after B meets C. A catches B if \(v_A>v_B\), while both velocities remain fixed.
Even if both are moving in the same direction, A can catch B if its signed velocity is greater.

blocks.title: Decide whether there is another contact
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after the B–C impact, C moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

After the B–C impact, decide whether A catches B while their velocities remain constant. Give the signed closing rate for A and the particle on its right, in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

fields.label: Does A catch the body ahead?

blocks.hint: A keeps the velocity it acquired in the first collision. Compare it with the neighbour’s latest velocity.
blocks.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(16\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(2)+(2)u=16\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact the momentum of B and C just before contact is \(12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)v+(4)(3)=12\]

B leaves this impact with signed velocity \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The measured velocity of C was \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

A keeps its velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The body on its right now has velocity \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The closing rate is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

It is positive, so A catches the body ahead.

sections.title: Where does the next gap come from?
sections.label: Time a re-contact
sections.intro: The A–B gap at the B–C impact is built up during the preceding interval. Use the first-stage separation rate over that interval.

blocks.html: After finding that gap, divide by the new closing rate to find the time from the second impact to the predicted re-contact.
Do not use the initial B–C gap as the A–B re-contact gap.

blocks.title: Find the time from the second impact to the next contact
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the first impact the gap between B and C is \(12\,\mathrm m\). Immediately after the B–C impact, C moves to the right at \(\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

It is known that A catches B after the B–C impact. Give the time in seconds from the B–C impact to that next contact.

fields.label: Time after the B–C impact in seconds

blocks.hint: Compute the A–B gap at the moment of the second impact before calculating another time.
blocks.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(16\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(2)+(2)u=16\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact the momentum of B and C just before contact is \(12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)v+(4)(\frac{10}{3})=12\]

B leaves this impact with signed velocity \(- \frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The measured velocity of C was \(\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The B–C impact occurs \(2\,\mathrm s\) after the first impact. During that time A and B have separated by \(8\,\mathrm m\).

The gap now closes at \(\frac{8}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so divide the current gap by that rate to obtain \(3\,\mathrm s\).

sections.title: How can I audit the whole record?
sections.label: Use the total as a cross-check
sections.intro: Keep the total for all three particles as a final consistency check. It cannot replace each pair’s equation or the contact ordering.

blocks.html: In a smooth horizontal model the total for A, B and C is the same across both impacts. You still check separation and each subsequent approach separately.
An unchanged overall total is compatible with many different impact sequences.

blocks.title: Decide whether there is another contact
blocks.prompt:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. extraPractice.prompt:
Three particles \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), in that left-to-right order, have masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and move on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightwards as positive. Initially \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) move to the right at \(10\), \(1\) and \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), respectively. Immediately after hitting \(B\), \(A\) has velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After the subsequent \(B\)–\(C\) impact, \(C\) has velocity \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Find the signed closing rate of \(A\) relative to \(B\) after the second impact. Does \(A\) catch \(B\) while these velocities remain constant?

fields.label: Does A catch the body ahead?

extraPractice.hint: At the second impact, include the incoming momentum of \(C\). Then subtract the final velocity of \(B\) from that of \(A\).
extraPractice.solution:
At the first impact, \(3(10)+2(1)=3(3)+2u\), so the velocity \(u\) of \(B\) after that collision is \(\frac{23}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

At the next impact, \(2(\frac{23}{2})+4(1)=2v+4(5)\). Thus the new velocity of \(B\) is \(v=\frac72\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The closing rate is \(3-\frac72=-\frac12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The gap is increasing, so \(A\) does not catch \(B\).

Write a separate line for each impact

Use the same signed axis throughout. On a smooth line, a body outside the collision retains its velocity.

If B is behind C and \(v_B>v_C\), a gap \(d\) closes after \(\Delta t=\frac{d}{v_B-v_C}\).
